operations.evidence: HMICFRS inspects each police force's crime data integrity roughly every three to five years
the interval means inspection findings are not continuous monitoring
HMICFRS samples incidents using opening codes where a crime would be expected
the audit tests a sample rather than every incident
crime-recording accuracy is checked for violence against the person, sexual offences and all other offences; fraud is excluded because it is recorded only by the City of London Police
the three-group framework is not an offence-level parcel measure
HMICFRS weights inspection results to calculate accuracy for each offence group and all crime excluding fraud
weighted inspection accuracy is not the same as a crime rate
the graded judgement uses recording accuracy plus dip samples, recording timeliness and force management and oversight
the grade must not be interpreted from accuracy percentage alone
HMICFRS estimated 80.5% accuracy with a plus-or-minus 2.0 percentage-point interval in 2014 for all crime excluding fraud
the estimate belongs to the 2014 inspection design
HMICFRS estimated 92.4% accuracy with a plus-or-minus 0.3 percentage-point interval by the end of the 2021 to 2022 programme
later inspections are affected by 2023 counting-rule changes
17 of 23 inspected forces recorded more than 90% of reported crime in the 2021 to 2022 programme
not all forces were inspected in that programme
6 of 23 inspected forces recorded more than 95% of reported crime in the 2021 to 2022 programme
the count is programme-specific and not a current league table
HMICFRS inspections use a subset of crimes from the most recent three months
the findings are a single-point snapshot and cannot provide continuous accuracy
changes to Home Office Counting Rules mean 2023 to 2025 and later inspection findings are not directly comparable with earlier findings
cross-cycle performance comparisons must remain fail-closed
regular external auditing reintroduced in 2014 was a key driver of crime-data-integrity improvements
association with improvement does not isolate a single causal effect
senior leadership and chief constables play a critical role in setting data culture and driving recording improvements
governance evidence is qualitative and force-specific
well-recording forces commonly use crime-data standards or integrity boards with senior officer representation
board presence alone does not prove accurate recording
clear separation between crime-recording teams and performance teams reduces manipulation or gaming risk; an independent force crime registrar increases data integrity
organisational separation is a control, not a measured crime outcome
regular training and clear guidance support more accurate and consistent recording; training has addressed burglary, theft-from-person and domestic-abuse recording issues
training effectiveness varies by implementation and force
many consulted forces view a dedicated central crime-management unit as best practice
the review sample covered nine forces and may not generalise to all forces
centralised crime-management units give forces greater control over data quality than relying only on frontline entry
centralisation does not validate every record automatically
a smaller dedicated recording team is more likely to apply counting rules consistently than thousands of frontline officers
the claim is a process rationale rather than a national effect estimate
centralisation is not the only recording model and does not by itself guarantee accurate and consistent recording
candidate scoring must not treat centralisation as a force-quality proxy
crime volume and resource constraints can prevent forces from validating every crime record
absence of full validation does not identify which individual records are wrong
recording and validating crime close to the initial call can improve control but requires significant resource
point-of-call use varies by force
44 police forces may manage crime recording in different ways
national aggregation can conceal force-level process variation
recording decisions, guidance changes, IT systems and quality assurance all influence police-recorded-crime quality
the factors can interact differently across forces and over time
Metropolitan Police recorded about one-sixth of all crimes excluding fraud and computer misuse in the year ending December 2023
quality issues in a large force can disproportionately affect national totals
operational administrative data cannot have all inaccuracies and inconsistencies eliminated
quality controls reduce but do not remove residual error
domestic-abuse flags are manually applied and can be interpreted inconsistently within and across forces
flag inconsistency affects contextual classification rather than proving offence absence
online-crime flags are also often applied inconsistently within and across police forces
online flags must not be assumed complete
different stalking categories carry different maximum sentences; recording the wrong category can allocate the case to the wrong type of investigator
classification error is an operational-quality risk, not a parcel-risk value
regional force-crime-registrar groups discuss counting-rule interpretations to support consistent application
regional agreement cannot eliminate all national variation
force registrars can seek advice from the National Crime Registrar; queries and answers are shared on a Police Digital Service knowledge platform
advice availability does not prove uniform implementation
